body:
Cybercrime and cybersecurity incidents

Cybercrime involves conduct that constitutes an offence under applicable criminal law and is committed using, targeting or involving computer resources. Examples include online impersonation used for cheating, identity theft and certain forms of unlawful digital harassment.

A cybersecurity incident and a cybercrime may occur together, but the terms are not synonymous. A system disruption may require urgent technical assistance even before its cause is established. A fraudulent call made through a digital service may require police investigation even though the victim's device was never hacked.

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) operates under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). Its scheme was approved on 5 October 2018, and it became an attached office of MHA on 1 July 2024.

I4C supports coordinated national action against cybercrime, including cooperation among law-enforcement agencies, reporting arrangements, analysis and capacity building. It assists in dealing with offences that may involve victims, accounts or offenders across different states.

I4C is not CERT-In. I4C's central emphasis is cybercrime coordination and support to law enforcement. CERT-In's central emphasis is national cybersecurity incident response and related advisories.

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP), available through the official government cybercrime reporting service, allows citizens to report cybercrime complaints. It covers different categories of cybercrime, with particular attention to crimes against women and children.

Complaints submitted through the portal are handled by the concerned State or Union Territory law-enforcement agency. Registration of an FIR, investigation, arrest and prosecution-related action are carried out by legally authorised agencies according to applicable law. A portal complaint does not automatically mean that an FIR has already been registered or that the allegations have been proved.

The 1930 financial cyberfraud helpline

The national helpline number 1930 is used for reporting financial cyberfraud. The Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS), launched in 2021 under I4C, supports prompt reporting and coordination intended to prevent or limit further movement of fraudulently transferred funds.

Quick reporting may improve the opportunity for protective action, but fund recovery is not guaranteed. Citizens should provide accurate transaction information through official channels and continue with the complaint procedure communicated by the competent authorities.

Gujarat's role in cybercrime prevention and investigation

In Gujarat, the State Cyber Crime Cell, CID Crime, Gujarat Police, and other competent state police units form part of the state's arrangements for preventing, detecting and investigating cybercrime. The State Cyber Crime Cell is based in Gandhinagar.

Cybercrime may cross district and state boundaries, so Gujarat Police can require cooperation with other state agencies and national coordination arrangements. Nevertheless, the existence of national infrastructure does not transfer every cybercrime investigation from the state police to I4C.

Illustrative citizen response

A resident of Surat receives a message that appears to be from a bank and, after following it, discovers an unauthorised transfer. The resident should promptly contact the relevant bank and report the suspected financial cyberfraud through 1930 and the official national cybercrime reporting arrangements. The matter may then require action by the competent Gujarat police unit and participating financial institutions.

If, instead, a citizen encounters a false video about a public announcement without an identifiable criminal offence, the appropriate first response may be verification and platform reporting rather than assuming that a criminal investigation must follow.

Prelims focus

  • I4C functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
  • I4C became an attached office of MHA on 1 July 2024.
  • NCRP is the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.
  • 1930 is the national financial cyberfraud reporting helpline.
  • CFCFRMS was launched in 2021 to support action against financial cyberfraud.
  • Trap: National complaint coordination does not replace investigation by the competent State or UT police.

[Ministry of Home Affairs, Cyber and Information Security Division, 'Overview about the I4C', consulted 16 November 2026; MHA, Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 5184, answered 24 March 2026, measures concerning I4C, NCRP and CFCFRMS; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, citizen reporting information, consulted 16 November 2026; Gujarat Police, State Cyber Crime Cell, CID Crime, official Gujarat cybercrime website, organisational and contact information, consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
The main statutory framework

The Information Technology Act, 2000 is an important Indian law concerning electronic records, computer-related wrongdoing and specified responsibilities of digital intermediaries. It has been amended since its original enactment, including significant provisions introduced through the 2008 amendment.

For preliminary examinations, the task is to connect each important section with its actual subject. Cybercrime, blocking of online information, protection of critical systems and intermediary liability are related but legally distinct matters.

Important provisions and their functions

ProvisionMain subjectEssential distinction
Section 43Specified unauthorised acts affecting computer resourcesProvides for compensation or liability in the circumstances stated in the Act.
Section 66Computer-related offencesDeals with specified Section 43 acts committed dishonestly or fraudulently.
Section 66CIdentity theftFraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature.
Section 66DCheating by personationCheating by impersonation using a computer resource or communication device.
Section 66EViolation of privacyAddresses specified unlawful capture, publication or transmission of images of a person's private area.
Section 69ABlocking public access to informationAuthorises specified blocking action subject to statutory grounds and safeguards.
Section 70Protected systems and critical information infrastructureConcerns designated protected computer resources and the definition of critical information infrastructure.
Section 70ACritical infrastructure protection agencyStatutory basis for NCIIPC.
Section 70BNational cybersecurity incident-response agencyStatutory basis for CERT-In.
Section 79Intermediary liability exemptionConditional protection for qualifying third-party information, subject to statutory conditions.

Identity theft and cheating by personation

Sections 66C and 66D should not be treated as identical. Section 66C concerns fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's specified identification features. Section 66D concerns cheating through impersonation using a computer resource or communication device.

For example, use of another person's password without authorisation may raise identity-theft issues under the relevant facts. A fraudulent online message that impersonates a bank representative to deceive a customer may raise cheating-by-personation issues. Whether a particular offence is established requires the complete statutory ingredients and evidence.

Section 69A and the blocking of information

Section 69A empowers the Central Government or authorised officers, subject to prescribed safeguards, to direct blocking of public access to information in specified circumstances. Safeguards include written reasons, ordinarily a hearing for the identified originator or intermediary, committee scrutiny, approval by the Secretary, MeitY, and review at least once every 2 months. The statutory grounds include the sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order and prevention of incitement to the commission of a cognizable offence relating to those grounds.

This is a specific legal power, not a general rule allowing every disputed opinion to be blocked. A platform's removal of content under its own policies must also be distinguished from statutory blocking under Section 69A.

Section 79 and intermediary liability

Section 79 provides a conditional exemption from liability for certain third-party information hosted or transmitted by intermediaries. It is not unrestricted immunity. An intermediary must satisfy the statutory conditions, including relevant due-diligence obligations, and the exemption is unavailable if the intermediary conspires in, abets, aids or induces the unlawful act, or fails to remove or disable access to unlawful material expeditiously after legally valid actual knowledge while preserving the evidence.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (24 March 2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 79 subject to its interpretation of the actual-knowledge requirement. The judgment linked legally relevant takedown knowledge to a court order or appropriate government notification concerning unlawful material within the applicable constitutional framework. The detailed intermediary rules have subsequently been amended, including in 2026.

The constitutional boundary: Shreya Singhal

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act because it violated freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) and could not be justified under Article 19(2). The Court upheld Section 69A and the associated Blocking Rules, 2009, recognising the statutory safeguards.

Section 66A is not a valid offence. It must not be confused with Sections 66, 66C or 66D, which address different computer-related conduct.

Prelims focus

  • 66C: Identity theft; 66D: Cheating by personation using a computer resource.
  • 69A: Statutory power to block public access to specified information.
  • 70A: NCIIPC; 70B: CERT-In.
  • 79: Conditional intermediary liability exemption.
  • Shreya Singhal (2015): Section 66A struck down; Section 69A upheld.
  • Trap: Section 66A should never be presented as an operative cybercrime provision.

[Information Technology Act, 2000, India Code text, sections 43, 66, 66C, 66D, 66E, 69A, 70, 70A, 70B and 79; Supreme Court of India, Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, judgment dated 24 March 2015, reported at (2015) 5 SCR 963, findings on sections 66A, 69A and 79; MeitY, Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code Rules, 2021, consolidated text updated 10 February 2026; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: IT Act sections grouped by cyber offences, blocking, intermediary exemption and cybersecurity agencies, with Section 66A struck down in 2015.
pictures.caption: Cyber offences, blocking powers and institutional provisions serve separate purposes.

title: The Information Technology Act, 2000: Offences, Blocking and Legal Safeguards

body:
Why personal data protection matters

Digital services commonly process information relating to identifiable people. This may include names, contact details, account information and other information that identifies an individual directly or indirectly. Misuse or unauthorised disclosure can expose individuals to impersonation, fraud, harassment or interference with privacy.

Protection of personal data is different from checking whether a social media claim is true. A statement may be factually correct yet unlawfully disclose private information. Similarly, a false social media claim may be harmful even when no personal database has been accessed.

Privacy as a constitutional right

In Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge Bench of the Supreme Court recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right protected under the Constitution, including Article 21 and other relevant freedoms in Part III.

Article 19(1)(a) protects freedom of speech and expression. Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions by law on specified grounds, including the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.

Freedom of expression, privacy and public safety must be considered together when regulating digital communication. An important principle is that restrictions on rights must have a lawful and constitutionally supportable basis.

Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Act 22 of 2023, received presidential assent on 11 August 2023. Its framework concerns the processing of digital personal data for lawful purposes while recognising the interests and rights of individuals.

Important statutory terms

TermMeaning
Digital personal dataPersonal data in digital form.
Data PrincipalThe individual to whom personal data relates; for a child below 18, includes the parents or lawful guardian, and for a person with disability, includes the lawful guardian acting on that person's behalf.
Data FiduciaryA person who determines the purpose and means of processing personal data, alone or with others.
Data ProcessorA person who processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.
Consent ManagerA person registered with the Board to enable Data Principals to give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.

For example, a digital service deciding why and how it collects users' personal information may be a Data Fiduciary. A separate service processing that information on its behalf may be a Data Processor. The distinction depends on the actual roles performed, not merely on the names used by the organisations.

The Act's substantive framework

The Act provides a framework for lawful processing, consent and specified legitimate uses. Its substantive provisions include obligations concerning protection of personal data, breach notification, additional responsibilities regarding children's data and rights relating to access to information, correction, erasure and grievance redressal.

These are features of the enacted statutory framework. Their legal operation must be understood in light of the phased commencement dates below. It would be inaccurate to assume that every such obligation or right had already commenced by November 2026.

Phased commencement: the essential date distinction

The Central Government notified commencement arrangements through G.S.R. 843(E), dated 13 November 2025. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, notified through G.S.R. 846(E) on the same date, also have phased commencement.

DateProvisions commencingPrincipal significance
13 November 2025Specified institutional, definitional and enabling provisions of the Act; Rules 1, 2 and 17–21Initial legal and institutional framework, including provisions concerning the Data Protection Board of India.
13 November 2026Act Sections 6(9) and 27(1)(d); Rule 4Consent Manager-related provisions and their registration framework commence.
13 May 2027Principal remaining processing, consent, obligations and individual-rights provisions; Rules 3, 5–16, 22 and 23Main substantive data-processing framework is scheduled to commence.

Status at the content cutoff, 16 November 2026: The initial institutional provisions and the Consent Manager-related provisions have commenced. The main substantive processing duties and individual-rights provisions scheduled for 13 May 2027 have not yet commenced.

Data Protection Board of India

Section 18 provides for the establishment of the Data Protection Board of India. The Board is the specialised statutory body envisaged for functions such as considering matters and inquiries assigned to it under the Act. The relevant provisions operate according to their individual commencement dates.

It is important to distinguish this institution from CERT-In and the police. A question concerning lawful personal-data processing belongs to the data-protection framework. A reportable cybersecurity incident may involve CERT-In. An alleged criminal impersonation or online fraud may require police action. The same real-world occurrence can engage more than one framework, but each body retains its distinct function.

Prelims focus

  • Puttaswamy (2017): Privacy recognised as a fundamental right by a 9-judge Supreme Court Bench.
  • DPDP Act, 2023: Act 22 of 2023; assent on 11 August 2023.
  • Data Principal: Individual concerned; Data Fiduciary: Determines purpose and means of processing.
  • Section 18: Establishment of the Data Protection Board of India.
  • 13 November 2026: Consent Manager-related commencement; 13 May 2027: scheduled commencement of main substantive provisions.
  • Trap: Enactment in 2023 did not bring every DPDP provision into force immediately.

[Supreme Court of India, Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, constitutional recognition of privacy; Constitution of India, Articles 19(1)(a), 19(2) and 21; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Act 22 of 2023, sections 1–2, 6, 7–18 and 27; MeitY, commencement notification G.S.R. 843(E), 13 November 2025, clauses (a)–(c); MeitY, Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025, rule 1(2)–(4) and rule 4; official texts consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Digital Personal Data Protection and the Constitutional Right to Privacy
